chapter_theme: The second run of the description of Hemangadam: the harvest of red paddy from reaping to threshing, the cane presses and the carts of goods, then the pools, groves, houses and mansions of its towns, its pleasures, its daily thousands of feedings and charities, and a closing claim that it is a place for penance and for wealth alike, as if heaven had come down to earth.
structure_note: Verses 54 to 64 describe the fields (harvest 55 to 59, cane 60, carts 61 to 63, a summary 64); 65 to 74 the pools, groves and houses; 75 to 77 the towns' charity and pleasures and a closing estimate of the land. No character acts and nothing happens.

54.reading: The narrator says the wealth of the land, where not a space the size of a fish's eye lies empty, with cane groves swarming with bees and paddy fields tall enough to hide famed elephants, cannot be told to those with eyes of flesh, so loud is its din.
54.nuance: ஊன் கணார் (those with eyes of flesh) sets ordinary sight against a fuller seeing: the poet opens the description by declaring it beyond telling, the standard figure of the country-praise section, and then tells it for twenty-four verses.

55.reading: The field labourers, having drunk filtered toddy and wearing honey-dripping blue lilies, take the iron sickle shaped like a waning crescent in their right hands and reap the broad field of red paddy.
55.nuance: The reapers (மள்ளர்) drink toddy before work and the Jain poet records it without comment; the sickle is seen as a waning moon, the first of many sky images in the section.

56.reading: With strong hands they reap so that the lotuses droop and the lilies wither, the clamour swells, the flowering pond echoes and the young birds start up, and they stack the cut paddy like hills and pass the curved sickles from hand to hand.
56.nuance: The labour is shown through its cost to the pond flowers and fledglings, a small note of damage within the praise of plenty. கம்பலம் is taken here as clamour; the word division of line 2 is not certain.

57.reading: As bands of young men carry off their heavy loads of sheaves, shoals of vaalai fish flee headlong, bee-opened lotuses are torn on their stalks, and the areca palms with their spathes shed their nuts.

58.reading: The stacks rise as if crossing the heads of the raining clouds, pressing on the clean ground, and the long threshing floors, strewn with bursting jackfruit full of rich segments, are crowded and gleam with stacks.
58.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are compressed: it is not clear whether it is the stacks or the clouds that press on the ground and roar (நரல), and the reading given is one way of construing them.

59.reading: Having trodden out the great stacks with buffalo bulls, winnowed the grain aside, cleared the straw and let the wind take the chaff, they pile the red paddy in heaps that look like high-peaked hills of rich gold.
59.nuance: The verse walks through the stages of threshing in order, and only at the end turns grain into gold: the plenty is earned by a sequence of work before it becomes an image of wealth.

60.reading: At every press where cane is crushed, those who come eagerly drink the juice, and the sweet smoke from boiling what is left over rises into the sky until the sun turns red.
60.nuance: The juice is drunk by whoever arrives (விரும்பி வந்து அடைந்தவர்), with no word of payment or of a giver: the land's surplus is open to all before it is boiled down.

61.reading: So that the distress of the kinai-drum bards is brought low, there are carts carrying red paddy from the granaries, carts loaded with sugarcane, and carts carrying flowers for weddings through the streets.
61.nuance: The first line takes up the Sangam figure of the hungry bard whose want a patron ends, but no patron is named: here it is the traffic of the land's carts that puts the bards' distress down.

62.reading: There are carts of tender coconuts from the rich coconut palms, carts of soft betel leaves, carts of clusters of ripe areca nuts, and carts that roll along laden with sweet goods.

63.reading: There are carts that come groaning with the wealth of the dark sea, carts packed full of pulses and many other noisy carts, and they are said to crowd every direction in good order.
63.nuance: என்பவே (they say) marks the catalogue of carts (61 to 63) as report, keeping the poet's claim of a land beyond telling.

64.reading: The rich fields, adorned with marutham trees where parrots grow and never touched by ruin, are said to be like this every day, and the bright settlements ringed by groves that never stop dripping honey stand beyond description.
64.nuance: கேடு இலா (without ruin) and வைகலும் (every day) make the plenty permanent, not seasonal: the closing verse of the field description claims a land with no bad year.

65.reading: In the groves the swan-cocks carry off the fresh petals opened from the lotus to build their nests, as if at a wedding where flowers were the flawless golden lamps, the cool koel the drum, and the feathered peacock and the bees on the branches led in the marriage.
65.nuance: The grove stages a wedding among birds, each creature given a role in the rite; the line division of 3 and 4 makes it uncertain which creature plays which part beyond the lamp and the drum.

66.reading: In the pond, among blue lilies like the eyes of lovers met together, vaalai fish leap over the withered vallai creepers, and the heron watching them looks like one watching a dancing woman leap along a rope with her many ornaments ringing.
66.nuance: The simile turns the heron, usually a hunter of fish, into a spectator at a rope-dance; the fish are safe for the length of the image.

67.reading: When women with eyes like blue lilies plunge into the pools, the strings of their many-stranded girdles, worn over cloth as fine as breath, break and scatter, and since no one cares to gather them, every pool wears gold and looks like the sky in bloom with stars.
67.nuance: கொள்ளும் நீரர் இன்மையின் (because there is none who would take them) is the point: the gold lies because no one in the land wants it, not because anyone guards it.

68.reading: The pestles of those pounding green rice flakes, as they swing, knock down plantains, jackfruits and mangoes and their sweet fruit, shake down the fruit of the swaying areca and coconut, and the fragrant screwpine and champak open their bright flowers as if laughing.
68.nuance: A hyperbole of crowding: the household's work and the orchard's fruit are so close that the pestle's swing harvests the trees.

69.reading: Buffaloes that have grazed the fragrant ponds come to the long houses with milk streaming from their great udders and wetting the ground, feed their calves, and pour out milk until the women's pots are full, and with them the rows of mansions are bright.

70.reading: Doves with beaks like split silver, red feet like threaded coral, eyes red as kunri seeds and bodies like gathered agil smoke drink milk together with the parrots, while the unfailing myna sings.
70.nuance: The milk of 69 is drunk by the house birds: the surplus feeds even the pets.

71.reading: The flower-scented smoke that perfumes the starched cloth sinks into the jewelled tresses of the fair women on the rows of mansions, and they look like peacocks gathered on a high-peaked hill, spreading their wings in the mist.
71.nuance: The mountain mist of the old simile is made here from the household's own incense: the women are peacocks on a hill whose mist is perfume smoke.

72.reading: Women sulking from the longing within them say to the men, 'Your loves are in your eyes; let desire end here,' and when the men seize their bright girdles the strings break and scatter, so that the courtyard looks as if fire that smelts countless gold had spilled there.
72.nuance: The sulk ends as a picture of spilled gold: the lovers' quarrel is told as part of the land's wealth, not as a private crisis. Whose eyes hold the rivals, and whether the line plays on the woman's own reflection in the man's eye, the verse does not settle.

73.reading: Young horned rams, cocks with combs like plucked thonri flowers, water-fowl and the rest are set to fight by men who delight in such contests, and the uproar of their display and shouting, with the din of the festivals, is the only din the land knows.
73.nuance: The animal fights are offered as part of the land's pleasures, with no word against them, in a work held to be Jain where harm to living beings is the gravest wrong; the verse makes no claim either way. The sense of வேட்டவற்றின் ஊறு உளார் and வெருளி and the construction of line 4 are uncertain.

74.reading: When slender-waisted women spray from their mouths the toddy raised in cups, the young punnai trees burst into flower, winged bees sing the sevvazhi tune, and throughout the mansions they dwell like the stars of the sky at the eaves.
74.nuance: The verse uses the convention that a tree flowers when a woman sprays it with wine from her mouth. Line 4 (அரம்பை முலையின் இருந்தவே) is obscure: who dwells like stars, and whether அரம்பை is the plantain or the celestial dancer, is not clear.

75.reading: The towns brim with halls barred to no one, cool water from springs of the three fruits against the heat, flower-decked pavilions of sandal paste, the dances of women with killing spear-like eyes, and besides these every delight on earth of the five senses.
75.nuance: Open charity (விலக்கு இல் சாலை யாவர்க்கும்) and the pleasures of the five senses (ஐம் பொறி) stand in one list; the Jain epic praises the land for both without ranking them.

76.reading: Every day there are a thousand feedings and a thousand works of charity, a thousand adornments made by creeper-like women, a thousand auspicious rites with tireless craftsmen, and a thousand other things kept up by those who keep them.
76.nuance: Charity is counted in the same unit (ஆயிரம்) as adornment and ceremony: giving is a daily quantity of the land's life, kept up like its other works.

77.reading: The land is a place for those who do good penance and for those who do penance, for those who make good wealth and for those who make wealth, as if heaven, to make men long for the joy won there, had gladly fallen to earth, and it rests with the other lands circled about it.
77.nuance: The verse gives the land room for penance and for wealth alike, with no ranking. The contrast of நல்தவம் with தவம் and நல் பொருள் with பொருள் is not explained; one possibility is merit already earned against merit being made, another is good against ordinary pursuits. Heaven is pictured as the joy that penance earns, come down to make men want it, but the verse states no doctrine of how it is won. The repeated மற்ற நாடு of line 4 is obscure.

links.note: The Kural defines a land as where unfailing yield, the worthy (தக்கார்) and the undiminished wealthy gather; the Cintamani's closing verse on Hemangadam makes it a place for those who do penance and those who make wealth, after ten verses of harvest.
links.teaches: The epic fills the couplet's three-part definition with a whole country, and reads its worthy ones as those who do penance, so the Kural's land is given room for renunciants beside the wealthy.

gains.a: the hyperbole of heaven fallen to earth is anchored in a received Tamil definition of what makes a land
gains.b: the couplet's unspecified தக்கார் receives a concrete reading as ascetics living alongside the rich

links.note: The Kural calls those lands whose riches need no seeking; the Cintamani's pools are strewn with gold beads from broken girdles that no one troubles to gather.
links.teaches: Set beside the reapers and threshers of 55 to 59, the gold no one picks up shows the epic taking unsought wealth to mean surplus beyond need after labour, not riches without work.

gains.a: the image of the gold-starred pools is read as a mark of the ideal land rather than as mere ornament
gains.b: the couplet's riches that need no seeking are given a scene where the absence of seeking is visible

links.note: Puhar's open court leaves traders' bundles unguarded because a thief is made to carry his load and whirl; Hemangadam's pools hold gold that lies untaken because no one wants it.
links.teaches: Two epics praise a city by its untaken wealth but give opposite grounds, fear of a punishing power in the Silappathikaram and simple satiety in the Cintamani, so the marvel is not one convention but two theories of order.

links.note: The Sirupanarruppadai paints the kinai bard's hunger in his kitchen, his wife boiling unsalted greens behind a shut door, until a patron's gifts end it; the Cintamani puts the porunar's distress down in half a line, through the carts of paddy and cane.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam bard's want only to cancel it at once, and moves its relief from one named patron's gift to the anonymous traffic of a rich land.

gains.a: the stock phrase about the kinai bards is seen to carry a whole earlier genre of hunger and rescue
gains.b: the guide poem's patron-centred relief is set against a later picture where plenty, not a giver, ends the bard's want

links.note: The Perumpanarruppadai's girls on sky-touching terraces move like peacocks rejoicing on a great hill's slope; the Cintamani's women on the mansion rows look like peacocks spreading their wings in the mist on a high hill.
links.teaches: The epic inherits the Sangam figure of terrace women as hill peacocks but makes the hill's mist out of the houses' own perfume smoke, turning a natural setting into manufactured luxury.

gains.a: the simile is traced to an older description of a port city's rich women
gains.b: the older image is shown surviving into the epics with its landscape replaced by the household

links.note: In both the sulking woman's charge turns on eyes: in the Kural all women feast on the man with theirs, in the Cintamani the women say his loves are in his eyes, and refuse him.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the eye-charge inside the couple's quarrel, while the epic lets the same charge end in snapped girdles and spilled gold, so the sulk becomes a sign of the city's wealth rather than a turn in a love.

gains.a: the epic's brief quoted words are recognised as a set move of the sulking wife
gains.b: the couplet's private reproach is shown being absorbed into public description of a prosperous land

source_issues: 75 line 2: தணீர் is probably தண்ணீர் with a lost letter.
73 line 1: கொய் மலர தோன்றி looks like a mis-division of கொய்ம்மலர்த் தோன்றி.
74 line 4: அரம்பை முலையின் இருந்தவே is obscure as printed; the construction may be corrupt.
77 line 4: the repeated மற்ற நாடு is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
